method: Built on proven learning methods: explain it simply first (Feynman technique), see it as a picture (dual coding), learn from worked examples, then test yourself (active recall), mix topics and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).

overview.bigIdea: Motion is simply **change of position with time**. This whole chapter is one ladder: each step asks “how fast is the previous thing changing?”

ladder.a: Distance + direction from a reference point

languages.name: Words
languages.text: Define it exactly: distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration.

languages.name: Graphs
languages.text: Slope gives a rate. Area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.

languages.name: Equations
languages.text: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as (constant acceleration only).

plan.text: Lessons 1–4. Read the hook, learn the core ideas, cover the answer and redo each worked example.
Lessons 5–6. Sketch every graph yourself before reading about it.
Lessons 7–8. Solve the worked examples with the GUFS method, then take a Check knowledge quiz.
Smart revision sheet after 1 day, 3 days and 7 days. Mixed quiz (all topics) before the exam.

lessons.title: Describing position and motion
lessons.hook: A friend phones: “Where are you?” You say “200 metres.” That answer is useless — 200 m **from where**, and **in which direction**? Physics needs exactly those two things to describe position.

core.def: A fixed point from which we measure positions.
The **distance and direction** of an object from the reference point at an instant of time.
An object is in motion if its position with respect to the reference point **changes with time**.
An object is at rest if its position with respect to the reference point **does not change** with time.
An instant is a single clock reading (t = 4 s). A time interval is the duration between two readings (from 4 s to 10 s = 6 s).

explain: On a straight line we use **signs for direction**: positions to the right of O are positive (+), to the left are negative (−). So −20 m means 20 m from O on the left.

**Rest and motion are relative.** A bag on a train seat is at rest for the passenger but moving for someone on the platform. A book on your table is at rest relative to the Earth, but the Earth moves around the Sun — so relative to the Sun the book is moving. Always ask: *relative to what?*

diagram.caption: Positions on a straight line: A is +100 m, B is +40 m, C is −20 m from the origin O.

example.q: The school gate is the origin. A shop is at +300 m and the bus stop is at −200 m. Describe the bus stop's position and find the distance between the shop and the bus stop.
steps: Bus stop: the number 200 gives distance, the minus sign gives direction → 200 m from the gate, on the side **opposite** to the shop.
Distance between them = 300 − (−200) = 300 + 200 = 500 m.
example.answer: 200 m from the gate, opposite side to the shop; 500 m apart.

mistakes: Giving position without direction (“40 m” instead of “+40 m” or “40 m east”).
Saying an object is “at rest” without saying relative to what.
Mixing up an instant (t = 5 s) with a time interval (5 s long).
lessons.tip: In any “is it at rest?” question, name the reference point in your first line. That line alone often earns the mark.
lessons.memory: Position = HOW FAR + WHICH WAY + FROM WHERE.
examAsk: Define motion and rest.
Can an object on the Earth be at rest? Explain (Revise, Reflect, Refine Q11).
Differentiate instant and time interval.

cards.q: Which two things describe the position of an object?
cards.a: Its distance and direction from a reference point, at an instant of time.

cards.q: A book lies on a table. Is it at rest?
cards.a: At rest relative to the Earth, but in motion relative to the Sun (the Earth moves). Rest and motion depend on the reference point.

cards.q: What does a negative position mean on a straight line?
cards.a: The object is on the negative side (usually left) of the origin.

lessons.title: Distance travelled and displacement
lessons.hook: Walk 5 steps forward and 5 steps back. Your legs did 10 steps of work (**distance**), but you are exactly where you started (**displacement = 0**). The fuel a scooter burns depends on distance; where it ends up depends on displacement.

core.def: The **total length of the path** covered. Only a numerical value (with unit), no direction. SI unit: metre (m).
The **net change in position** between two instants. Needs magnitude **and direction** — from the first position towards the second. SI unit: metre (m).
The numerical value (with units) of a quantity that also has a direction.
|Displacement| ≤ distance travelled. They are **equal only when the object moves in one direction without turning back**.

explain: Displacement ignores the path and looks only at start and end. That is why it can be **zero** even when a lot of distance is covered (a ball thrown up and caught, a round trip home–shop–home).

Quantities that need only a number (distance, speed, time) are called *scalars*; quantities that need a number **and** a direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration) are called *vectors*. You will study these names in higher classes — for now just remember which ones need a direction.

diagram.caption: The athlete in Fig. 4.4: distance = 100 m + 60 m = 160 m, but displacement = 40 m in the positive direction.

example.q: A student runs from the ground floor to the 4th floor of a school, then comes down to the 2nd floor. Each floor is 3 m high. Find the total vertical distance and the displacement. (Revise, Reflect, Refine Q2)
steps: Draw a vertical line: ground = 0 m, 4th floor = 4 × 3 = 12 m, 2nd floor = 2 × 3 = 6 m.
Distance = up 12 m + down (12 − 6) = 6 m → 12 + 6 = **18 m**.
Displacement = final − initial = 6 m − 0 m = **6 m upwards** (direction included!).

mistakes: Writing displacement without direction — you lose the mark.
Thinking displacement can never be zero, or can be bigger than distance.
Adding distances for displacement: displacement is final position minus initial position, not a sum of paths.
lessons.tip: Draw a quick number line for every distance/displacement question. It takes 10 seconds and prevents most errors.
lessons.memory: Distance = what the LEGS feel. Displacement = what the MAP shows (start → end arrow).
examAsk: Can displacement be zero when distance is not? Give an example.
Father goes home → shop → home → shop → home (Q1): distance and displacement.
Fuel used depends on distance or displacement? Justify.

cards.q: A ball is thrown up and caught at the same point. Displacement?
cards.a: Zero — it ends where it started.

cards.q: When are distance and |displacement| equal?
cards.a: When the object moves in a straight line in one direction without turning back.

cards.q: Can |displacement| be greater than distance?
cards.a: Never. It can only be less than or equal to the distance.

lessons.title: Average speed and average velocity
lessons.hook: Sarang swims to the far end of a 25 m pool and back in 50 s. He is exhausted, his average speed is 1 m s⁻¹ — yet his average velocity is **zero**. Understanding why is the whole lesson.

core.def: **Total distance travelled ÷ time interval.** Only a numerical value, no direction.
**Displacement (change in position) ÷ time interval.** Has magnitude and direction (+ or − on a straight line). vₐᵥ = s/t
SI unit of both: m s⁻¹ (m/s). Also km h⁻¹.
Equal distances in equal intervals of time (constant speed). Unequal distances → non-uniform motion.
Change in a quantity ÷ time taken. Average velocity is the average rate of change of position.

explain: Speed tells you **how fast**; velocity tells you **how fast and which way**. For motion in one direction on a straight line, average speed = magnitude of average velocity.
The speedometer of a vehicle shows (nearly) the speed at an instant; the direction the tyres point gives the direction of velocity at that instant.

table.title: Memorise: km h⁻¹ → m s⁻¹ (multiply by 5/18)
head: km h⁻¹

example.q: On a road trip you drive 200 km north in 3 hours and then 200 km south in 2 hours. Find the average speed and average velocity for the whole trip. (Pause and Ponder 4)
steps: Given: distance = 200 + 200 = 400 km; time = 3 + 2 = 5 h; you end where you started, so displacement = 0.
Average speed = 400 km ÷ 5 h = **80 km h⁻¹**.
Average velocity = 0 km ÷ 5 h = **0 km h⁻¹**.

mistakes: Averaging the two speeds: (66.7 + 100)/2 = 83.3 km h⁻¹ is WRONG here. Always use total distance ÷ total time (= 80 km h⁻¹).
Using displacement for speed or distance for velocity.
Forgetting to convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before using other SI values.
lessons.tip: Read the question word: “speed” → use distance; “velocity” → use displacement and state the direction.
lessons.memory: km/h → m/s: × 5/18. m/s → km/h: × 18/5. (36 km/h = 10 m/s is the easiest anchor.)
examAsk: When is average velocity zero but average speed not zero? (Pause and Ponder 5)
Two postmen problem (Example 4.1).
Convert 54 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.

cards.q: Average speed formula?
Average velocity formula?
When does |average velocity| equal average speed?
cards.a: When the object moves in one direction along a straight line.

cards.q: 72 km h⁻¹ in m s⁻¹?

lessons.title: Average acceleration
lessons.hook: That jolt you feel when a bus starts suddenly or brakes hard? That is your body sensing **acceleration** — a change in velocity. A bus cruising smoothly at 80 km h⁻¹ gives no jolt: fast, but **zero acceleration**.

core.def: **Change in velocity ÷ time interval.**  a = (v − u) / (t₂ − t₁)
m s⁻² (m/s²).
Speeding up → acceleration in the **same** direction as velocity (+). Slowing down → **opposite** to velocity (−).
A change in the **magnitude** of velocity, its **direction**, or both.
An object dropped from a height gains 9.8 m s⁻¹ every second: constant acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻², downwards.

explain: Acceleration does not depend on how fast you move, but on **how quickly your velocity changes**. A bus at a high constant velocity has zero acceleration.
Constant acceleration: velocity changes by **equal amounts in equal intervals of time**. In this chapter we only deal with constant acceleration.

example.q: A bus at 36 km h⁻¹ speeds up to 54 km h⁻¹ in 10 s. Later it brakes from 54 km h⁻¹ and stops in 5 s. Find the average acceleration in both cases. (Example 4.3)
steps: Convert: 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹, 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹.
Speeding up: a = (15 − 10) / 10 = **0.5 m s⁻²** (in the direction of velocity).
Braking: a = (0 − 15) / 5 = **−3 m s⁻²**. The minus sign means acceleration is opposite to velocity.

mistakes: Not converting km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ — the answer comes out 3.6 times too big.
Dropping the minus sign when the object slows down.
Believing “high speed = high acceleration”.
lessons.tip: Always write u and v first, both in m s⁻¹. Then a = (v − u)/t. Keep the sign in the final answer and say what it means.
lessons.memory: Velocity is to position what acceleration is to velocity: each one is “how fast the previous one changes”.
examAsk: Can a scooter with constant speedometer reading accelerate? (Q3)
Car from rest to 24 m s⁻¹ in 6 s: find acceleration (Q4).
Direction of acceleration when slowing down.

cards.q: SI unit of acceleration?
A car moves at a constant 20 m s⁻¹ on a straight road. Acceleration?
Can there be acceleration at constant speed?
cards.a: Yes, if the direction of motion changes (e.g. turning, circular motion).

lessons.title: Position–time graphs
lessons.hook: A graph is a story told in a picture. A position–time graph is **not a map** of the road — it shows how far from the origin the object is at every instant.

core.def: Time on the X-axis, position on the Y-axis. Choose a scale that uses most of the graph paper.
Equal displacements in equal times → **constant velocity**.
Position does not change → object **at rest**.
Velocity increasing → **accelerated motion**.
Slope = BC/CA = (s₂ − s₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = **velocity**. A steeper line means a higher velocity.

lessons.graphCaption: Three motions on one position–time graph: flat = at rest, straight = steady, curving up = speeding up.
explain: To find velocity from the graph, pick two points A and B on the line, draw a right-angled triangle ABC, and divide the rise BC by the run CA. Read the values carefully off the axes.
If two objects are plotted on the same axes, the one with the **steeper** line covers more displacement in the same time interval, so it has the higher velocity.

example.q: On a position–time graph, the vehicle is at 40 m at t = 2 s and at 80 m at t = 4 s (Fig. 4.14). Find its velocity.
steps: Change in position BC = 80 m − 40 m = 40 m.
Change in time CA = 4 s − 2 s = 2 s.
Velocity = slope = 40 m ÷ 2 s = **20 m s⁻¹**.

mistakes: Reading the graph as the path of the object.
Dividing a single position by a single time on a curve — always use a change between two points.
Missing labels and units on the axes when plotting (easy marks lost).
lessons.tip: When plotting, write a scale in the corner (e.g. X-axis: 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis: 5 divisions = 20 m), label both axes with quantity and unit, and join points smoothly.
lessons.memory: Flat = sat (at rest). Straight = steady. Curving up = speeding up. Slope = speed of change.
examAsk: Plot a position–time graph from a table and find velocity.
Compare two objects A and B from their graphs (Fig. 4.16, Q6).
What does a line parallel to the time axis mean?

cards.q: Slope of a position–time graph gives?
Position–time graph parallel to the time axis?
Curved position–time graph getting steeper?

lessons.title: Velocity–time graphs
lessons.hook: Same idea, one level up. On a velocity–time graph the **slope** tells you acceleration and the **area** under the line tells you displacement. Two readings from one picture — examiners love this.

core.def: Constant velocity, **zero acceleration**.
Velocity increasing with **constant acceleration** (same direction as velocity).
Velocity decreasing with **constant acceleration opposite** to velocity (negative).
Slope = (v − u)/(t₂ − t₁) = **acceleration**.
Area between the line and the time axis = **displacement** in that time interval.

lessons.graphCaption: Car starting from rest (Table 4.5). Slope = 0.5 m s⁻²; shaded area = displacement.
explain: Why is area = displacement? For constant velocity, the area is a rectangle: velocity × time = displacement. For changing velocity, split the area into a rectangle and a triangle (or use the trapezium formula).
Units check: (m s⁻¹) × (s) = m. If your area does not come out in metres, something is wrong.

example.q: A car starts from rest and speeds up uniformly to 20 m s⁻¹ in 5 s, travels at 20 m s⁻¹ for 10 s, then brakes uniformly and stops in 6 s. Find the total distance travelled. (Revise, Reflect, Refine Q9)
steps: Sketch the v–t graph: a triangle (0–5 s), a rectangle (5–15 s), a triangle (15–21 s).
Total distance = 50 + 200 + 60 = **310 m**.

mistakes: Using the slope for displacement or the area for acceleration.
Finding area on a position–time graph (it means nothing there).
Forgetting the ½ in the triangle area.
lessons.tip: For multi-stage motion, always sketch the v–t graph first, split it into rectangles and triangles, and label each area with its value. Examiners give step marks for this.
examAsk: Find acceleration and displacement from a v–t graph (Fig. 4.17, 4.18).
Cyclist graph: shade areas and find displacement (Q12).
Two cars from rest: plot v–t graphs and compare (Q15).

cards.q: Slope of a velocity–time graph gives?
Area under a velocity–time graph gives?
A v–t graph sloping downwards in a straight line means?
cards.a: Velocity decreasing with constant acceleration opposite to velocity.

lessons.title: Kinematic equations
lessons.hook: When acceleration is constant, just five quantities describe the motion: **s, u, v, a, t**. Know any three and the equations give you the other two. This is where most numerical marks are.

core.def: Velocity after time t (from the definition of acceleration).
Displacement in time t (area under the v–t graph).
Links velocity and displacement **without time**.
s = ½(u + v)t and s = vt − ½at² (from The Journey Beyond).
Valid only for **constant acceleration** in a straight line. Signs of u, v, a, s show direction.

table.title: Pick the equation by the quantity you DON'T have
head: Missing
Use

explain: **Decode the hidden information** in the question: “starts from rest” → u = 0; “comes to rest / stops” → v = 0; “uniform velocity” → a = 0; “dropped” → u = 0 and a = g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Use the **GUFS method** for every numerical: **G**iven (convert to SI), **U**nknown, **F**ormula, **S**ubstitute and solve — then write the answer with unit and direction.

example.q: A bus travels at 36 km h⁻¹. The driver sees an obstacle 30 m ahead and takes 0.5 s to react before braking. The brakes give a constant acceleration of −2.5 m s⁻². Will the bus stop before the obstacle? (Revise, Reflect, Refine Q10)
steps: Given: u = 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹, reaction time = 0.5 s, a = −2.5 m s⁻², v = 0.
Reaction distance (no braking yet, constant velocity) = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m.
Braking distance: v² = u² + 2as → 0 = 10² + 2(−2.5)s → s = 100/5 = 20 m.
Total stopping distance = 5 + 20 = **25 m**, which is less than 30 m.
example.answer: Yes — it stops after 25 m, 5 m before the obstacle.

mistakes: Using these equations when acceleration is not constant.
Forgetting the minus sign for braking (a is negative).
Forgetting reaction distance in stopping-distance questions.
Not converting km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.
lessons.tip: Braking distance ∝ u² (from v² = u² + 2as). Double the speed → four times the braking distance (Example 4.8: 28.1 m at 54 km h⁻¹, 112.5 m at 108 km h⁻¹). Use this to check answers and in “safe distance” reasoning questions.
lessons.memory: “Rest → u = 0. Stop → v = 0. Steady → a = 0. Drop → a = g.”
examAsk: Derive v² = u² + 2as or s = ½(u + v)t (trapezium area).
Motorbike at 28 m s⁻¹ stops in 98 m: find a and t (Q5).
Truck slows from 54 to 36 km h⁻¹ in 36 s: find distance (Q8).

cards.q: Which equation has no t?
“Starts from rest” means?
Speed doubles, same braking. Braking distance?
Condition for using kinematic equations?

lessons.title: Motion in a plane and uniform circular motion
lessons.hook: Spin a marble around the inside of a ring, then lift the ring. The marble does **not** keep circling — it shoots off in a straight line. It was being forced to turn all along. That turning is a change of velocity: **acceleration**.

core.def: Motion in two dimensions, e.g. a vehicle overtaking, a kicked ball, a satellite.
Distance = circumference = **2πR**; displacement = **0** (back to the start).
vₐᵥ = 2πR / T, where T is the time for one revolution. Average velocity over one revolution = 0.
Motion on a circular path with **constant speed**.
The **direction** of velocity changes continuously (it is along the tangent), so velocity changes → acceleration, even at constant speed.

explain: Think of an athlete on a rectangular track: 4 turns per round. A hexagonal track: 6 turns. Keep adding sides and the track becomes a circle — now the athlete is turning **all the time**, so the direction of velocity changes continuously.
Uniform circular motion is an idealised model. Real motions (planets around the Sun, a car on a circular turn) are close to it, which is why it is so useful.

example.q: Rohan studies from 6 PM to 7:30 PM. The minute hand of the clock is 7 cm long. For its tip, find the distance travelled and the displacement. (Take π = 22/7) (Revise, Reflect, Refine Q16)
steps: In 90 minutes the minute hand makes 1½ revolutions.
After 1½ turns the tip goes from “12” to “6” — opposite ends of a diameter. Displacement = 2R = **14 cm** (from 12 towards 6).
Average speed = 66 cm ÷ 90 min ≈ 0.73 cm per minute.

mistakes: Saying “constant speed, so no acceleration” in circular motion.
Writing displacement after one full circle as 2πR (it is 0).
Using 2πR for half a revolution (it is πR; displacement 2R).
lessons.tip: For clock or merry-go-round questions, first count how many revolutions happen, then use: full turn → displacement 0; half turn → displacement 2R.
lessons.memory: Same speed, changing direction → STILL accelerating.
examAsk: Why is uniform circular motion called accelerated motion?
Distance and displacement for a clock hand (Q16).
Marble and ring activity (Activity 4.5).

cards.q: Distance in one revolution of radius R?
Displacement after one full revolution?
Is uniform circular motion accelerated? Why?
cards.a: Yes — the direction of velocity changes continuously.

cards.q: Direction of velocity at a point on the circle?
cards.a: Along the tangent at that point, in the direction of motion.

formulas.name: Graph rules
formulas.f: p–t slope = v;  v–t slope = a;  v–t area = s

revision: Position = distance + direction from a reference point. Rest and motion are relative.
Distance = total path (no direction). Displacement = final − initial position (with direction).
|Displacement| ≤ distance. Equal only for one-direction straight-line motion.
Average speed = distance/time. Average velocity = displacement/time. Round trip → average velocity 0.
Acceleration = (v − u)/t, unit m s⁻². Slowing down → negative (opposite to velocity).
Constant velocity → zero acceleration, however fast. Change in direction alone → acceleration.
Free fall: velocity increases by 9.8 m s⁻¹ every second → g = 9.8 m s⁻².
p–t graph: flat = rest, straight = constant velocity, curve = acceleration; slope = velocity.
v–t graph: flat = constant velocity; slope = acceleration; area = displacement.
v = u + at;  s = ut + ½at²;  v² = u² + 2as — constant acceleration only.
Rest → u = 0; stop → v = 0; steady → a = 0; dropped → a = g.
Stopping distance = reaction distance (u × reaction time) + braking distance (u²/2|a|).
Braking distance ∝ u²: double speed → 4× distance.
Circle: one revolution → distance 2πR, displacement 0; half → πR and 2R. Average speed 2πR/T.
Uniform circular motion is accelerated: velocity direction changes continuously (along the tangent).

numerical: **G**iven: list every value with its symbol and convert to SI units (km h⁻¹ → m s⁻¹, minutes → s).
**U**nknown: write what is asked, e.g. “s = ?”. Decode hidden values (rest, stop, dropped).
**F**ormula: write the equation in symbols before numbers. Pick it by the missing quantity.
**S**ubstitute and solve: show one clean substitution line — this line earns step marks.
Box the answer with **unit and direction** (and sign meaning, e.g. “− means opposite to velocity”).
**Sense check**: braking distance should grow with speed; a car's acceleration of 50 m s⁻² is suspicious.
graph: Read the axes first: position–time or velocity–time? This decides whether the slope means velocity or acceleration.
For slope: choose two points far apart on the line, draw the triangle, write rise ÷ run with units.
For area: split into rectangles and triangles, label each area, add them.
When plotting: title, labelled axes with units, a stated scale, points marked clearly, smooth line.
writing: Definitions: use the exact textbook words (“net change in position”, “change in velocity divided by time interval”).
“Give reason” answers: state the rule, then apply it to the case in one line.
Differences (distance vs displacement, speed vs velocity): make a 3-row table — definition, direction needed?, can it be zero?
Use a small labelled diagram (number line, triangle on a graph) whenever it helps — it is quick and scores.
checklist: I can define position, displacement, average speed, average velocity and average acceleration.
I can explain why rest and motion are relative.
I can find distance and displacement for round trips and stair/floor problems.
I can convert km h⁻¹ ↔ m s⁻¹ quickly.
I can find acceleration with the correct sign and explain the sign.
I can read velocity from a position–time graph (slope).
I can read acceleration (slope) and displacement (area) from a velocity–time graph.
I can choose the right kinematic equation and solve with GUFS.
I can calculate stopping distance including reaction time.
I can find distance, displacement and average speed for circular motion and explain why it is accelerated.
